hero.heading:
Call for Civic Hosts:
The Public Assembly on AI
hero.intro:
Over the past year, the BLOOM Project and local partners developed a community assembly model that combines digital tools with deliberative public problem-solving. We tested it in two pilots in Utah and Oregon, engaging nearly 1,000 people across six counties on questions about AI.

Now we’re inviting a cohort of Civic Hosts to help build the Public Assembly on AI: a network of communities across the United States working out what they want from AI and building the civic power to realize it.

moment.heading: The choices AI raises are already on the table.

items.label: Where we live
items.question: Should our county approve a data center, and on what terms?

items.label: Learning & work
items.question: What rules should govern AI in our schools and workplaces?

items.label: Who benefits
items.question: Who should share in the gains from AI, and who bears the risks?

moment.contrast: Polls capture what people think in isolation. Social media rewards what divides us.
moment.bridge: Communities need a way to navigate these choices together, and the power to see them through.

ladder.heading: The Public Assembly on AI helps communities decide together the future worth building, from local to national.
ladder.body:
Many communities struggle to have a say even in local choices, like whether a data center gets built. On state and national questions, a single community’s voice rarely carries.

The Public Assembly helps each community set its own agenda and be heard at home, and connects communities that find common cause so they can advance change together. Along the way, informed dialogue builds the relationships that make change last.

tiers.body: Hosts bring their communities together to find common ground and act where they can.
Shared priorities across communities set the agenda for state-level representative assemblies.
Questions that need further action shape a national civic assembly on AI, bringing local perspectives to the national stage.

work.heading: Two kinds of community assembly.
work.intro: Every host is supported to run a community assembly, in one of two forms. We’ll match each host to the form that fits its community, its capacity, and what’s at stake, and co-design the details together.

core.name: Short arc

steps.name: One-to-ones
steps.body: Conversations that bring local leaders into the inquiry on a pressing AI issue.

steps.name: Community forums
steps.body: 30–50 residents meet to sort out local priorities, name local actions, and flag what needs state action.

steps.name: Open poll
steps.body: Engage hundreds of residents to create a map of the opinion landscape, including common ground.

steps.name: Results
steps.body: A map of community priorities that are immediately actionable and what needs further deliberation.

core.outcome: Works towards a map of community priorities: what’s immediately actionable, and what needs further deliberation.

coDesign.name: Long arc

steps.name: Goal setting
steps.body: Community forum and open poll rounds surface shared values, ending in a goals statement the community stands behind.

steps.name: Idea development
steps.body: Additional community forum and open poll rounds develop potential solutions.

steps.name: Tradeoffs
steps.body: Residents weigh options together, producing a map of tradeoffs to carry into decision making.

steps.name: Decision making
steps.body: Recommendations are drafted, tested for broad agreement, and put to a public ratification vote.

coDesign.outcome: Works towards community recommendations, tested for broad agreement and put to a public ratification vote.

tools.heading: CivicOS: BLOOM’s open-source deliberation platform
tools.intro: Every Civic Host gets lifetime access to CivicOS and training on how to use it.

items.label: Live conversations
items.name: Table Themer
items.body: Captures what each table says during community forums and civic assemblies, and shows the themes emerging across the room as the conversation happens.
items.imageAlt: Residents talking around a table at a community forum

items.label: Digital participation
items.name: Open Poll
items.body: Residents add their own statements and react to their neighbors’ (agree, disagree, or unsure), mapping where the community agrees, where it divides, and what common ground already exists.
items.imageAlt: An Open Poll statement on a phone, with agree and disagree votes around it

items.label: Reports & insights
items.name: Public reports
items.body: Turns everything people said into a clear public report that decision-makers and neighbors can read in minutes.
items.imageAlt: Cover of the public report: What did Central Oregonians have to say about AI?

support.heading: Funding, tools, and a network behind you.

receive.name: Methods
receive.body: A playbook built from our pilots in Utah and Oregon, refined with and for this cohort.

receive.name: Platform
receive.body: CivicOS tools for live conversations, open polls, and public reports. More on the tools below.

receive.name: Training
receive.body: Facilitation and organizing, plus coaching, through your civic hub or BLOOM.

receive.name: A peer cohort
receive.body: A national network of hosts on the same timeline, plus a state or regional cluster where there’s a civic hub.

impact.heading: What your community’s work can impact.

items.name: Government policy
items.body: Every host identifies decision-makers and decisions on a timeline: a county commission vote, a district’s classroom policy, an employer’s deployment plan, a state bill. What the community concludes is delivered to those decision-makers in public.

items.name: Community action
items.body: Much of what a community decides it wants needs no official’s permission: workplace monitoring policies, a parent council adopting school guidance, a library running AI literacy sessions.

items.name: Agency & connection
items.body: Participants leave with the experience of making a difference in their community, practice in deliberation and facilitation, and relationships with neighbors they would not otherwise have met.

who.heading: What makes a strong host.
where: Ideal hosts work where something clear is at stake: a decision about AI that a nameable body will make on a nameable timeline, or a plan to put a missing decision on the table.
who.topicsIntro: Hosts choose the issues most relevant to their community.
topics: AI in K–12 and higher education

criteria.name: Existing relationships and convening capacity
criteria.body: Enough standing with enough different people to convene partners: faith, labor, youth and education, small business, neighborhood and civic, or whoever the real constituencies are where you are.

criteria.name: A commitment to collaborative politics
criteria.body: Drawn to finding out what people think through deliberation, rather than confirming what you already believe.

criteria.name: Organizing or policy capacity
criteria.body: Hosts who know local decision-makers and can turn people out through their networks will likely be more successful. BLOOM helps with synthesis, reporting, and pathways to impact.

criteria.name: A learning partner
criteria.body: This is a first cohort. We’re looking for hosts who will try things, tell us plainly what isn’t working, and help shape the model for the communities that come next.

hub.heading: Already supporting a network of local civic organizations?
hub.body: Some organizations bring several hosts together across a state or region with the capacity to coach them, stand behind the quality of their work, and help carry what their communities conclude to state decision-makers. If that’s you, let’s talk about serving as a state or regional civic hub.
hub.button: Inquire about joining as a civic hub

timeline.heading: From application to a national assembly.

notes.name: Selection process
notes.body: Short-listed finalists are invited to interviews in December. Being invited is not a guarantee of selection.

notes.name: The arc
notes.body:
Short arc assemblies run 12 weeks between February and July 2027, with staggered starts; long arc assemblies run across the full window.

Together, this network will have the opportunity to commission state or national assemblies on AI in 2028.
